terms.definition: A network-attached, persistent block storage service for EC2 instances. Data survives instance stop/reboot/termination.
terms.example: Like an external USB hard drive plugged into your laptop over Wi-Fi — you can unplug it and plug it into another laptop.

terms.definition: A temporary, physically attached disk on the same host machine as the EC2 instance. Data is lost when the instance stops or terminates.
terms.example: Like the RAM-drive or internal SSD soldered directly onto a laptop motherboard — fast, but lost if the machine dies.

terms.definition: A single block storage device created in EBS that can be attached to an EC2 instance. Similar to a hard disk.
terms.example: Like a 20 GB hard disk you buy, format, and attach to your server.

terms.definition: Input/Output Operations Per Second — measures how many read/write operations a storage device can handle per second.
terms.example: Databases need high IOPS because they read/write many small chunks rapidly.

terms.definition: The rate of data transfer, measured in MB/s. Matters for workloads that read/write large sequential blocks of data.
terms.example: A 100-file transfer where each file is 1 MB gives 100 MB/s throughput at 100 IOPS.

terms.definition: General Purpose SSD — the second-generation EBS SSD. IOPS are tied to volume size (3 IOPS per GB, max 16,000).
terms.example: Default choice for web servers, dev/test environments, and most standard workloads.

terms.definition: General Purpose SSD — third generation. IOPS and throughput are configurable independently of storage size. 20% cheaper than gp2.
terms.example: AWS recommends migrating from gp2 to gp3 for better performance and lower cost.

terms.definition: Provisioned IOPS SSD — highest performance EBS type. Supports up to 64,000 IOPS. Used for mission-critical, latency-sensitive databases.
terms.example: Oracle, SQL Server, or high-frequency trading platforms running on EC2.

terms.definition: Throughput Optimized HDD — low-cost HDD for frequently accessed, throughput-intensive workloads. Max 500 IOPS, 500 MB/s throughput.
terms.example: Big Data, Hadoop clusters, data warehouses that do large sequential reads/writes.

terms.definition: Cold HDD — lowest cost EBS type for infrequently accessed data. Max 250 IOPS, 250 MB/s throughput.
terms.example: Log archives, backup storage, compliance data rarely accessed after initial write.

terms.definition: A point-in-time, incremental backup of an EBS volume stored durably in Amazon S3. Used for backups, AMI creation, and cross-AZ/Region migration.
terms.example: Taking a photo of your hard disk at 3 PM — you can restore to exactly that state later.

terms.definition: After the first full snapshot, subsequent snapshots only store blocks that have changed — saving time and cost.
terms.example: If you change 2 GB of data on a 20 GB volume, the next snapshot stores only those 2 GB.

terms.definition: A software configuration template for an EC2 instance containing the OS, pre-installed software, and optionally data volumes.
terms.example: Like a factory reset image for your laptop — includes Windows + all drivers pre-installed.

terms.definition: An isolated data center location within an AWS Region. EBS volumes are AZ-specific — they can only attach to EC2 instances in the same AZ.
terms.example: Mumbai Region has 3 AZs: ap-south-1a, ap-south-1b, ap-south-1c.

terms.definition: A high-performance journaling filesystem used by default on Amazon Linux 2. EBS volumes can be formatted with XFS before use.
terms.example: When you run mkfs.xfs /dev/nvme1n1, you prepare the disk so Linux can store files on it.

terms.definition: A widely used Linux filesystem (fourth extended filesystem). An alternative to XFS for formatting EBS volumes.
terms.example: Common on older Linux distributions and often used for non-Amazon Linux EC2 instances.

terms.definition: A Linux command that lists all block devices (disks and partitions) attached to the instance, including their mount points and sizes.
terms.example: Running lsblk after attaching a new EBS volume shows the new device (e.g., /dev/nvme1n1) ready to be formatted.

terms.definition: A Linux command that grows an XFS filesystem to fill the available space on a partition after a volume resize.
terms.example: After expanding an EBS volume from 8 GB to 20 GB, run sudo xfs_growfs -d / to claim the new space.

terms.definition: A Linux utility that extends a partition to use additional space on a disk — run before xfs_growfs when scaling up a root volume.
terms.example: sudo growpart /dev/nvme0n1 1 extends partition 1 of the nvme0n1 disk.

terms.definition: An EBS volume setting that controls whether the volume is automatically deleted when its attached EC2 instance is terminated. Root volumes have this enabled by default; additional volumes do not.
terms.example: If you set Delete on Termination = No, the EBS volume survives after you terminate the EC2 instance — but you'll keep paying for it.

terms.definition: Increasing the size or performance of a single existing EBS volume — e.g., growing from 8 GB to 20 GB.
terms.example: Your website is growing and the 8 GB root disk is getting full — you scale up to 20 GB without replacing anything.

terms.definition: Attaching additional EBS volumes to an EC2 instance and combining them into a larger logical storage unit.
terms.example: Instead of one 40 GB volume, attach four 10 GB volumes and combine them using LVM for a total 40 GB pool.
